title: "The NixOS Module System Architecture"

# The NixOS Module System Architecture

Managing operating systems traditionally means editing scattered files in `/etc/`, running systemctl commands, and hoping different configuration files don't conflict. The boring default of NixOS is: **the Module System — a typed, declarative framework where options define what can be configured, and configurations merge automatically into a single unified system generation**.

## Mental model

A NixOS module is a function that returns an attribute set with two primary keys:
1. **`options`:** Declares configuration settings, their types (`lib.types.str`, `lib.types.bool`), default values, and documentation.
2. **`config`:** Defines the concrete values or sets up systemd services, users, and files based on whether options are enabled.

```
Module A (declares services.desk.enable) ──┐
                                          ├──► Module System (merges & type-checks) ──► Final System
Module B (enables services.desk.enable) ──┘
```

The module system handles priority resolution (`lib.mkDefault`, `lib.mkForce`), conditional enabling (`lib.mkIf`), and deep merging across all imported files.

## Worked examples

### Case 1: Minimal Self-Contained Module

Save as `desk_module.nix`. A custom module defining a desk service option.

```nix
# desk_module.nix
{ lib, config, pkgs, ... }:

let
  cfg = config.services.deskOperations;
in
{
  options.services.deskOperations = {
    enable = lib.mkEnableOption "Desk operations automation daemon";

    port = lib.mkOption {
      type = lib.types.port;
      default = 8080;
      description = "TCP port the desk daemon listens on.";
    };

    banner = lib.mkOption {
      type = lib.types.str;
      default = "Desk Operational";
      description = "Welcome banner message displayed on startup.";
    };
  };

  config = lib.mkIf cfg.enable {
    environment.systemPackages = [
      (pkgs.writeShellScriptBin "desk-banner" ''
        echo "${cfg.banner} on port ${toString cfg.port}"
      '')
    ];
  };
}
```

When `services.deskOperations.enable = true;` is set anywhere in your machine configuration, the script is built and injected into `environment.systemPackages`.

### Case 2: Priority Resolution with mkDefault and mkForce

Save as `priorities.nix`. Manage base corporate defaults that individual hosts can override.

```nix
# priorities.nix
{ lib, ... }:

{
  # Default fallback that can be overridden by specific hosts
  networking.hostName = lib.mkDefault "generic-desk";

  # Forceful override that wins over standard values
  services.openssh.enable = lib.mkForce true;
}
```

`lib.mkDefault` sets lowest priority (easily overridden), while `lib.mkForce` sets highest priority (overrides standard values).

## The trap

Defining custom options without specifying types (`type = lib.types.anything;`). Without types, invalid configuration values (like passing a string where a port number is required) fail silently until runtime instead of during early evaluation.

**The fix:** Always declare strict types (`lib.types.bool`, `lib.types.port`, `lib.types.listOf lib.types.str`).

## The boring rule

- Group reusable system configuration into modules.
- Guard implementation logic with `config = lib.mkIf cfg.enable { ... };`.
- Use `lib.mkDefault` in shared baseline profiles so individual machines can customize them.

## Try this

1. In `desk_module.nix`, add an option `workers = lib.mkOption { type = lib.types.int; default = 4; };` and interpolate it into the script.
